title: The Retrieval Scorecard

post.author: u/night_bench_ysbel
post.title: I'm the night examiner at a firearms lab. Since the upgrade, our report search feels better to everyone. Tonight it buried the one report that mattered.

blocks.text: I'm the night examiner at the Calderbrook Firearms Laboratory. We never see what happened. We see what is left: the small brass case a gun throws out when it fires, called a cartridge case. Each gun scratches its own marks into the brass, like a signature. An examiner lays two cases side by side under a microscope and writes down whether the marks match. That write-up is a comparison report.

We have thousands, so nobody reads them all. We search them. You paste in a description, and the case-file search hands back every report in order, best match first. That is a ranked list, and a report's place in it is its rank. Our screen shows the first five. A system that finds documents and puts them in order like this is called a retrieval system.
Last month the company that sells ours, Sightline, upgraded it. Everyone says it feels better. The first result is more often the report you wanted.

Tonight Lowri Haverstock, our senior examiner, stopped at my bench with a report she had just finished. "I've seen these marks before," she said. "Three years ago. Paper days." Until 2024 we wrote reports on paper. When we went digital, every old report was scanned: photographed page by page, then run through text recognition, software that reads the letters in a picture and turns them into text a search can read.

She was right. A scanned report from August 2023 describes the same gun. I pasted her new report's description into the search. First came D6, a digital report from this year that matches too. The 2023 report came ninth, four rows below the bottom of the screen. Our old search still runs on a test machine. It put that report second.
It felt better. It hid the one report that mattered.

I rang our lab manager. He wants to keep the new search, and he has numbers. Over the last week he had taken 7 recent reports and searched with each one's description; tonight he added Lowri's as the eighth. Each of those searches is a query. Lowri marked which of 12 older reports each query should find: its right reports. Five of the 12 are old scans, S1 to S5; the digital ones are D1 to D7. A set like that, with the right answers marked in advance by a person, is a labelled set: a golden set for a search. He counted one thing: how often each search put a right report first.
Each line below shows a query, the reports Lowri marked right, and the rank of the first right report in the old and the new search.

query  right reports  old  new
Q1     D6 S3          2    1    (tonight's)
Q2     D1 D3          2    1
Q3     S1 S4          1    2
Q4     D2             3    1
Q5     D4 S5          1    1
Q6     S2             2    6
Q7     D5 D7          1    1
Q8     D7 S1          2    1
first result right:   old 3 of 8   new 6 of 8
Six against three. He says that settles it, and he signs on Friday. But on Lowri's query, the report she needed sat below the screen, where nobody reads. What should I ask for before Friday?

The old search, on the test machine, ranks S3 2nd and D6 4th, so both are on the five-result screen. The new search, Sightline's upgrade, ranks D6 1st and S3 9th, so only D6 is on the screen and S3 sits four rows below it.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in your lab is haunted, not even the search. Your manager is grading a retrieval system, and the trade has words for it. A report is relevant to a query when Lowri marked it right. Precision at k asks: of the first k results, what share are right? His count, a right report first, is precision at 1. Recall at k asks it the other way round: of all the right reports, what share made the first k? Mean reciprocal rank, MRR, looks only at the first right result: score 1 divided by its rank (first place 1, second a half, sixth a sixth), then average over the queries. nDCG, short for normalized discounted cumulative gain, goes in steps: give every right result a point, shrink each point the lower it sits, add them up, then divide by what a perfect order would score. Each one answers a different question. So, two of mine. How many results does an examiner read before deciding a search found nothing? And of the right reports the new search put lower, what kind of report was each one?

replies.author: u/night_bench_ysbel
replies.text: All five on the screen, every time. If none of the five matches, we write no link found and move on. The others it put lower, I haven't checked yet. Lowri's was a scan.

comments.author: u/top_three_searle
comments.text: I've run the search for an online shop for nine years. Nobody reads past the first three results; precision at 3 is the only number that matters, and the first result matters most of all. Your manager has the right instinct. The new search puts a right report first twice as often. One old scan on one query is an anecdote. Keep the new one and stop reading tea leaves.

comments.author: u/scan_room_wilf
comments.text: I did that scanning in 2024, two of us in a back room. We ran the pages fast, on a low quality setting, and the text recognition made a mess of the handwriting in the margins. The typed parts came out mostly fine. If the new search is fussier about messy text than the old one, the scans would suffer first. We could do them all again properly. It would take months.

reply.prompt: The lab manager signs off the new search on Friday. What should Ysbel ask for first? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Keep the new search: its first result is right more often, and that is what examiners read.
options.verdict: Measured the feeling, not the job
options.part2: We kept it. Lowri's 2023 report was pulled only because she remembered it. A month later I ran the manager's 8 queries again and read only what an examiner reads, the five results on the screen. On three of them a report Lowri marked right was below the screen: S3 9th on Q1, S4 7th on Q3, S2 6th on Q6. Every one was an old scan. Nobody had noticed, because on most queries the first result was right.
options.senior: The first result is what people notice, which is why the new search felt better. But an examiner's job is to find every link, and a missed link costs far more than one extra report to read. Choose the measure by the task: here, how many right reports reach the screen.

options.text: Ask the examiners to rate old and new search for a week, and keep whichever they prefer.
options.verdict: Nobody rates what they never saw
options.part2: We ran a week of ratings. Most examiners preferred the new search, and I understand why: the first result was right more often, and a rating records how a screen felt. Nobody rated Lowri's 2023 report, because nobody saw it. When I finally ran the manager's 8 queries, the new search had put three right reports below the screen, all of them old scans. The week had told us how the search felt, which we already knew.
options.senior: A preference measures how the first screen felt, not what is missing from it. People can't rate results they never see. Ratings are useful beside a labelled set, not instead of one.

options.text: Re-scan the old paper reports at a higher quality, so the search can read them properly.
options.verdict: Maybe the cure, but nothing to check it
options.part2: Wilf's team began re-scanning, starting with the 2023 drawer. Weeks in, the manager asked whether it was helping, and nobody could say: we had no score from before to compare with. When we did run the manager's 8 queries, the new search found 3 of the 6 right scans in its top 5, and the old search found all 6. The re-scan might close that gap. Now, at least, we can check.
options.senior: Re-scanning may well fix the cause, since messy text from text recognition is a likely reason the scans rank low. But it is slow and costly, and without a score taken before and after, nobody can tell whether it worked. Measure first, then fix, then measure again.

options.text: Score both searches on the labelled set by recall in the top 5, with old scans split out.
options.part2: I scored both searches on the manager's labelled set by recall at 5, then split it by type. All queries: old 0.94, new 0.75. Old scans: old 1.00, new 0.50. Digital: old 0.83, new 1.00. The new search was better on digital reports and worse on the scans, and all three reports it pushed below the screen were scans: S3, S4 and S2. The manager didn't sign. Sightline got the 8 queries and one condition: no upgrade goes in until its recall at 5 on old scans matches the old search's. Until then, any search for a report from before 2024 runs on both.
options.senior: Pick the measure that matches the job. Investigators need recall, because a missed link costs more than an extra report to read. Set k to what people actually read, five here. Then slice by document type, because an average can hide one kind of document losing badly. Keep the labelled set and run it on every upgrade.

sim.title: Score the two searches by hand
sim.lede: You're Ysbel at the bench, the night Lowri found the 2023 report. The scorecard holds the manager's labelled set: 8 queries, Q1 to Q8, each a recent report's description, over 12 older reports, S1 to S5 old scans and D1 to D7 digital. Lowri marked each query's right reports, 14 in all, as yes or no. Both searches rank all 12 reports for every query; those rankings are stated data, not a real search. Pick the search, k (how many top results count; 5, the size of the screen, to start), the measure to work out, a slice and a query. Recall at k is right reports in the top k divided by all the query's right reports. Precision at k is right reports in the top k divided by k. Reciprocal rank is 1 divided by the first right report's rank. nDCG at k adds 1 / log2(1 + rank) for each right report in the top k, where log2 of a number is the power of 2 that makes it, and divides by the same sum for a perfect order. Every score is the plain mean over the queries. A slice keeps the queries that have a right report of one type and counts only that type as right.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you open on the new search at k 5: recall 0.75, MRR 0.83, 11 of 14 right reports on the screen, and S3 9th on Q1. Switch to the old search: recall 0.94, MRR 0.67, S3 2nd. Set k to 3 and compare precision: 0.42 old, 0.46 new. Back at k 5, pick the old scans slice: recall 1.00 old, 0.50 new. Then digital: 0.83 old, 1.00 new. Pick nDCG at k on Q1 and check the hand sum: 1 / 1.631 = 0.61. Slide k to 10: both find all 14. Last, try each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing hid the report on purpose. The new search ranks digital reports better and old scans worse, so its first result was right more often while three right scans fell below the five-result screen. The manager measured the first result; the job needed recall in the top 5, split by document type.

steps.title: The parts being measured.
steps.text: Calderbrook's search is the looking-up half of the systems in LATENT Season 3. a3e01: retrieval-augmented generation, RAG, looks up passages and hands them to a language model to answer from; the lab's search stops after the looking up. a3e02: chunking cuts each report into pieces that are searched one at a time. a3e03: a vector database stores each piece as an embedding, a list of numbers for its meaning, and finds the nearest ones fast. a3e04: hybrid search runs a keyword search and a meaning search and merges the two lists. a3e05: a reranker takes the first results and scores them again, more carefully. An upgrade can change any of these parts. A change that helps clean digital text can hurt the messy text that text recognition made from the scans. Scoring the search before and after is how you find out.

steps.title: Recall and precision at k, worked on the set.
steps.text: Scoring a search on a labelled set goes in steps. First, run each query and keep the ranked list. Second, mark which results are right, from the labels. Third, work out the score for each query. Last, average over the queries. What can go wrong: a right report nobody labelled counts as wrong, and a k that isn't what people read measures the wrong screen. Recall at k is the share of a query's right reports that made the top k. On Lowri's query, Q1, the new search has D6 1st and S3 9th: 1 of 2 in the top 5, recall 0.50. The old search has S3 2nd and D6 4th: 2 of 2, recall 1.00. Averaged over all 8 queries, recall at 5 is 0.94 for the old search and 0.75 for the new. In counts, the old search puts 13 of the 14 right reports on the screen and the new one 11. Precision at k is the share of the top k that is right. At k = 3 the new search wins narrowly, 0.46 against 0.42: 11 right in 24 places against 10. Manning, Raghavan and Schütze's textbook notes that web surfers want the first page to be right, while professional searchers such as paralegals and intelligence analysts want as high recall as possible. An examiner hunting for a link is the second kind.

steps.title: Mean reciprocal rank: why it felt better.
steps.text: Reciprocal rank is 1 divided by the rank of the first right result: 1 for first, 0.5 for second, about 0.17 for sixth. Its mean over the queries is MRR. Old search, Q1 to Q8: 0.5, 0.5, 1, 0.33, 1, 0.5, 1, 0.5. They add to 5.33; divided by 8, that is 0.67. New search: 1, 1, 0.5, 1, 1, 0.17, 1, 1. They add to 6.67; divided by 8, that is 0.83. MRR rewards a right answer at the top and ignores everything after it, which is exactly how the new search felt. It can't see S3 at all: on Q1 the first right report, D6, was already first. The manager's count, the first result right on 6 of 8 queries against 3, is precision at 1, and it misses S3 the same way.

steps.title: nDCG: every right result counts, less the lower it sits.
steps.text: nDCG, short for normalized discounted cumulative gain, goes in steps. First, give each result a gain, its value: here 1 if it is right and 0 if not, because Lowri's labels are yes or no. Second, discount each gain by its place: divide it by log2(1 + rank). log2 of a number is the power of 2 that makes it: log2(2) is 1, log2(4) is 2. Third, add the discounted gains down to place k: that is the DCG at k. Fourth, do the same for the perfect order, every right report at the top: the ideal DCG. Last, divide the first by the second, so a perfect ranking scores 1. For Q1 at k = 5, new search: D6 at rank 1 gives 1 / log2(2) = 1, and S3 at rank 9 is outside the top 5 and adds nothing. The ideal is 1 + 1 / log2(3) = 1 + 0.631 = 1.631. nDCG at 5 = 1 / 1.631 = 0.61. Old search: S3 at 2 gives 0.631, D6 at 4 gives 1 / log2(5) = 0.431, so 1.062 / 1.631 = 0.65. Over all 8 queries, nDCG at 5 is 0.69 for the old search and 0.73 for the new: it leans toward the top too, so overall it also prefers the new search. What can go wrong: with yes-or-no labels it can't tell a matching report from one merely worth reading. Graded labels, such as 2 for the same gun and 1 for worth reading, are what it was built for.

steps.title: Slice by document type.
steps.text: A slice keeps the queries that have a right report of one type and counts only that type as right. Old scans, queries Q1, Q3, Q5, Q6 and Q8: recall at 5 is 1.00 for the old search and 0.50 for the new, 6 of 6 scans on the screen against 3 of 6. Digital reports, queries Q1, Q2, Q4, Q5, Q7 and Q8: 0.83 against 1.00, 7 of 8 against 8 of 8. The whole loss is in the scans. All three right reports the new search pushed below the screen, S3 9th, S4 7th and S2 6th, are scans. The overall 0.75 hid a slice where the new search finds half.

diagram.aria: The scorecard. The labelled set, 8 queries over 12 reports with 14 right reports, is run through both searches. Old search: recall at 5 0.94, MRR 0.67, precision at 3 0.42. New search: recall at 5 0.75, MRR 0.83, precision at 3 0.46. Split by document type, recall at 5 on old scans is old 1.00 against new 0.50, and on digital reports old 0.83 against new 1.00.

notes.text: the new search wins the first result and loses the scans

explain.caption: Read left to right. The same labelled set runs through both searches. Overall, the new search wins on MRR and precision at 3 and loses on recall at 5. Split by document type, the loss is all in the old scans: 1.00 against 0.50, while on digital reports the new search is ahead, 1.00 against 0.83.

fix.title: The fix: score by recall at 5, slice by type, and check every upgrade
fix.text: Keep the manager's labelled set and grow it: every link an examiner finds by memory becomes a new query, with its right reports marked. Choose the headline measure by the job. Examiners read the five results on the screen and must not miss a link, so the headline is recall at 5, with MRR and nDCG beside it to show order. Report every score overall and by slice, old scans and digital at least, and add a slice whenever a new kind of document arrives. Agree a pass bar in advance, such as recall at 5 on every slice no lower than the old search's, and run the set on every upgrade before it goes in, keeping each result. Until Sightline clears that bar on the scans, search reports from before 2024 with both searches.

limits: Eight queries is a small set: one query moves an average by an eighth. Treat a small gap as a hint, not a verdict, and grow the set with every link found by hand.
Labels come from one examiner and can be missing. A right report nobody marked counts as wrong, so recall is only as good as the labels. Have a second examiner check a sample.
Recall at 5 says nothing about order within the screen or about what sits below it. Pair it with MRR or nDCG, and change k whenever the screen changes.

head: Measure
What it asks
Here: old against new
Use it when
rows: People read one answer and act on it.
What share of the top 3 is right?
People read a few and stop, and reading a wrong one is costly.
What share of the right reports reached the top 5?
Missing one costs more than reading an extra one.
How high is the first right result?
Are the right results near the top, all of them counted?
Order matters, and labels are graded.

explain.seniorTake: Before you compare two searches, decide what the reader's job needs and measure that, at the k they actually read. Investigators need recall: a missed link costs more than an extra report to read. Report each score by slice as well as overall, because an average can hide a kind of document the search has stopped finding. Keep the labelled set and run it on every upgrade, so *it feels better* is checked against a number before it ships.

realWorld.title: Precision and recall, and who needs which
realWorld.text: Manning, Raghavan and Schütze's Introduction to Information Retrieval (Cambridge University Press, 2008), in its online edition, defines precision as the fraction of retrieved documents that are relevant, and recall as the fraction of relevant documents that are retrieved. It says typical web surfers would like every result on the first page to be relevant (high precision), while various professional searchers such as paralegals and intelligence analysts are very concerned with trying to get as high recall as possible. Individuals searching their hard disks are also often interested in high recall searches.

realWorld.title: A test collection: documents, queries and judgments
realWorld.text: The same book lists what a test collection needs: a document collection; a test suite of information needs, expressible as queries; and a set of relevance judgments, standardly a binary assessment of either relevant or nonrelevant for each query-document pair. It calls that decision the gold standard or ground truth judgment of relevance. Calderbrook's labelled set is a small one: 12 reports, 8 queries and Lowri's labels.

realWorld.title: Precision at k, and NDCG
realWorld.text: On ranked results, the book describes measuring precision at fixed low levels of retrieved results, such as 10 or 30 documents, and calls precision at k the least stable of the commonly used evaluation measures. It says NDCG is designed for situations of non-binary notions of relevance, and that its normalization factor is calculated to make it so that a perfect ranking's NDCG at k for query j is 1. Its formula divides each gain by log2(1 + m) for the document at rank m, the form this case uses.

realWorld.title: Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002: cumulated gain
realWorld.text: Kalervo Järvelin and Jaana Kekäläinen of the University of Tampere introduced the cumulated gain measures. They start from two observations: highly relevant documents are more valuable than marginally relevant documents, and the greater the ranked position of a relevant document, the less valuable it is for the user, because the less likely it is that the user will ever examine the document. A simple way of discounting, they write, is to divide the document score by the log of its rank, and by selecting the base of the logarithm, sharper or smoother discounts can be computed to model varying user behavior. Their original form leaves ranks below the base undiscounted; the textbook form above shifts the rank by one instead, so rank 1 is never discounted.

asked: How would you evaluate a retrieval system?
Recall or precision for this task?
interview.answer: Start from the job, not the measure. Ask who reads the results, how many they read, and what a miss costs. Then build a labelled set: real queries, with every right document marked in advance by someone who knows the domain, a few dozen to start, grown over time. Run each version of the search on it and score at the k people actually read. For finding every link, as investigators, lawyers or safety teams must, recall at k leads, because a miss costs more than an extra document to read. For an answer box where one right result is enough, MRR or precision at 1 lead. nDCG at k adds a discounted gain for each right result, dividing each by log2(1 + rank), and divides by the ideal order's score, so 1 is perfect; it shines with graded labels. Example: right reports at ranks 1 and 9, k = 5, gives 1 / 1.631 = 0.61. Report every score by slice, such as document type, language or age, because an average can hide one slice getting much worse. Last, run the set on every change, with a pass bar agreed in advance.

terms.def: A lab that examines guns, bullets and cartridge cases for the police and courts, to say which items came from which gun. Calderbrook's is one; people also call this work ballistics.
The examiner on the night shift at Calderbrook. Ysbel compares marks and runs the case-file search while the day staff are away.
The small brass case a gun throws out when it fires. The gun scratches its own marks into it, like a signature, so two cases can be compared.
An examiner's write-up of whether the marks on two items, such as two cartridge cases or two bullets, match.
A report on shots fired on purpose from a gun the police have taken in, to collect cases and bullets that can be compared with others.
Calderbrook's search over its reports: paste in a description and it ranks every report, best match first. Sightline upgraded it last month.
A system that finds the documents that fit a request and puts them in order, like a librarian pulling the likeliest files off the shelf. A search engine is one.
Search results in order, best first. A document's rank is its place in the list: 1 for first.
What you search with. Here, a report's description pasted into the case-file search. The labelled set has 8, Q1 to Q8.
A digital picture of a paper page. Calderbrook's old paper reports, from before 2024, were scanned so the search could read them.
Software that reads the letters in a picture of a page and turns them into text. On handwriting and quick, low-quality scans it makes mistakes. Also called OCR.
A report Lowri marked as one a query should find. Information retrieval calls it relevant to that query. Here a report is either relevant or not.
Queries with their right documents marked in advance by a person, kept to score every version of a search: a golden set for retrieval. The manager's has 8 queries over 12 reports.
How many of the top results a measure counts. Calderbrook's screen shows five results, so k = 5 matches what examiners read.
Of a query's right reports, the share in the top k, averaged over queries. Here it is against Lowri's labels, not against exact search as in a3e03.
Of the top k results, the share that are right, averaged over queries. Precision at 1 asks only whether the first result is right.
1 divided by the rank of a query's first right result: 1 for first, 0.5 for second, about 0.17 for sixth.
Reciprocal rank averaged over the queries. It rewards a right result at the top and ignores everything after it. Old search 0.67, new 0.83.
Normalized discounted cumulative gain: each right result's gain divided by log2(1 + rank), added over the top k, then divided by the same sum for a perfect order. 1 is perfect.
In nDCG, the value of one result: here 1 if it is right and 0 if not. With graded labels, a closer match gets a bigger gain.
DCG at k is the sum of the discounted gains in the top k. The ideal DCG is the same sum with every right result at the top. nDCG is one divided by the other.
The power of 2 that makes a number: log2(2) is 1, log2(4) is 2, log2(3) is about 1.585. nDCG divides each gain by log2(1 + rank).
Labels with levels instead of yes or no, such as 2 for the same gun and 1 for worth reading. nDCG was designed for them.
Part of a labelled set scored on its own, such as the queries whose right reports are old scans, so a loss in one part can't hide in the average.
The textbook name for a labelled set: documents, queries, and a judgment of relevant or not for each query and document pair.
The judgment of what is relevant that every search is scored against. Here, Lowri's labels.
A computer kept apart from daily work for trying things out. Calderbrook's still runs the old search.
A trained assistant to lawyers who searches documents and prepares cases. The textbook names them as searchers who need high recall.
Someone who gathers and studies information for a government or company to find links and threats. Another kind of searcher who needs high recall.
The study of finding documents that meet a need in a large collection, and ranking them. Search engines are its best-known use.
A program that runs a system on a labelled set and works out the scores, the same way every time. Build Night X2 builds one for the Nightwatch copilot.
The international standard for running an organisation so its work is reliably good. Clause 9.1 covers deciding what to monitor and measure, how, and when.

atWork: Look for a search, or a RAG system, at work that was upgraded and judged by feel. A common pattern: a team swaps in a new embedding model or adds a reranker, people say the answers seem better, and months later someone finds that a whole kind of document, such as old scanned files, emails or another language, has quietly dropped out of the top results. Ask four things. Who reads the results, how many do they read, and what does a miss cost? Is there a labelled set of real queries with the right documents marked, run on the old and new versions before the switch? Is the headline measure the one the job needs, recall at the k people read when every link matters, MRR when one right answer is enough? And are the scores split by slice, document type, age or language, with a pass bar for each? Build Night X2, after a5e04, builds an eval harness for the Nightwatch copilot; its retrieval scorecard is this one, run on every change. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO 9001:2015, the international standard for quality management, or working toward it, clause 9.1 (monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation) covers deciding what to monitor and measure, the methods, when to do it, and evaluating the results. A labelled set run on every upgrade, with its scores kept, is the kind of evidence it looks for, and far cheaper built in from the first version than assembled before an audit.

recall.prompt: Your company replaced the search behind its support assistant, which looks up past fault reports before engineers decide whether a product is safe. Staff say the new one feels better, because its first result is more often right. Half the old fault reports are photos of paper forms. Your manager asks you to confirm the upgrade. What do you do?

keyIdeas.idea: Build a labelled set of real queries with the right documents marked in advance, and run both searches on it
Measure recall at the k people actually read, because a missed report costs more than an extra one to read
Split the scores by document type, such as photographed forms against typed reports, so one slice can't hide in the average

recall.model: Before confirming, I'd build a labelled set: real queries from engineers, with every right fault report marked in advance, and run the old and the new search on it. I'd score recall at the number of results engineers actually read, say the top 5, because a missed fault report costs far more than an extra one to read. A first result that's right more often is precision at 1; it explains the good feeling, not the job. Then I'd split the scores by document type, the photographed forms against the typed reports, since text read from photos is often messy and an average can hide the slice that got worse. The upgrade goes in only if recall holds on every slice.

recall.prompt: A query has 4 right reports, and a search's top 5 holds 2 of them. What are recall at 5 and precision at 5, in that order?
recall.why: Recall at 5 divides the right reports found, 2, by all the query's right reports, 4: 0.50. Precision at 5 divides the same 2 by the 5 places looked at: 0.40. Swapping the two divisors gives 0.40 and 0.50.

recall.prompt: Explain nDCG at k to a teammate with a small worked example: how is it computed, and why does a perfect ranking score 1?

keyIdeas.idea: Each right result gets a gain, discounted by its rank with a logarithm, so lower results count for less
The discounted gains are added up over the top k: that sum is the DCG
Divide by the ideal score, the same sum for the perfect order, so a perfect ranking scores 1

recall.model: Give each result a gain: here 1 if it's right and 0 if not, or a grade if your labels are graded. Discount each gain by its place: divide it by log2(1 + rank), so a right result further down counts for less. Add them up over the top k; that sum is the DCG at k. Then work out the same sum for the ideal order, every right result at the top, and divide by it. A perfect ranking gets exactly its ideal sum, so it scores 1. Example: two right reports, one at rank 1 and one at rank 9, with k = 5. The DCG is 1 / log2(2) = 1, the ideal is 1 + 1 / log2(3) = 1.631, so nDCG at 5 = 1 / 1.631 = 0.61.

recall.prompt: Three queries find their first right result at ranks 1, 2 and 4. What is their mean reciprocal rank?
recall.why: The reciprocal ranks are 1, 0.5 and 0.25. They add to 1.75, and 1.75 divided by 3 is about 0.58. 2.33 is the mean rank, 0.43 is 1 divided by that mean, and 0.75 adds the second and third reciprocal ranks and never divides.

recall.prompt: An investigator's search shows five results, and a missed link between two cases costs far more than reading one extra report. Which number should decide between two searches?
options: Precision at 1: how often the first result is right
Recall at 5, worked out for each type of document as well as overall
Mean reciprocal rank over all the queries
The examiners' ratings after a week of use
recall.why: The job is to miss no link among the five results read, so the measure is the share of right documents that reach the top 5, and splitting by type stops a kind of document losing badly inside a good average. Precision at 1 and MRR only see the first right result; ratings record how the screen felt.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 6 months later. Sightline fixed the scans, and every upgrade since has been scored on the eight queries before it goes in. It has passed every time: on old scans, the new search now matches the old one's score in the top 5. Last month the lab moved the case-file search onto new tablets at each bench. Their screen shows three results, not five, and nobody changed the scorecard. Tonight Lowri found another link from memory, to a 2022 scan. The search had it just below the tablet's screen.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the scorecard keep passing while a link was missed, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The scorecard still counts the top 5, but examiners now see only the top 3, so k no longer matches what people read
Re-run the scorecard at the new k, by slice, on both searches, or show more results on the screen
Add the new link to the labelled set as a query, so the set keeps growing with real misses

coldCase.model: The scorecard measures the wrong screen. It still counts recall in the top 5, but examiners now read only the top 3, so a right report in 4th or 5th place passes the scorecard and is never seen. The k in the measure has to match what people read: set k to 3. I'd re-run the scorecard at recall at 3, by slice, old scans and digital, on both searches, and if recall at 3 isn't good enough, show more results on the tablet, let it scroll, or go back to five. And I'd add tonight's link to the labelled set as a new query, with its right reports marked, so the set grows with every real miss.

sources.title: Christopher D. Manning, Prabhakar Raghavan and Hinrich Schütze, Introduction to Information Retrieval (Cambridge University Press, 2008), online edition, section 8.3, Evaluation of unranked retrieval sets, read 14 October 2026: precision is the fraction of retrieved documents that are relevant; recall is the fraction of relevant documents that are retrieved; web surfers want high precision; paralegals and intelligence analysts want as high recall as possible

Manning, Raghavan and Schütze, Introduction to Information Retrieval, online edition, section 8.1, Information retrieval system evaluation, read 14 October 2026: a test collection is a document collection, a test suite of information needs expressible as queries, and a set of relevance judgments, standardly binary; the gold standard or ground truth judgment of relevance

Manning, Raghavan and Schütze, Introduction to Information Retrieval, online edition, section 8.4, Evaluation of ranked retrieval results, read 14 October 2026: precision at fixed low levels of retrieved results, such as 10 or 30 documents; the least stable of the commonly used evaluation measures; NDCG is designed for situations of non-binary notions of relevance; a perfect ranking's NDCG at k is 1; the gain is divided by log2(1 + m)

Kalervo Järvelin and Jaana Kekäläinen, Cumulated Gain-Based Evaluation of IR Techniques, ACM Transactions on Information Systems 20(4), October 2002, pages 422 to 446, read 14 October 2026: highly relevant documents are more valuable; the greater the ranked position, the less valuable; divide the document score by the log of its rank; the base of the logarithm gives sharper or smoother discounts to model varying user behavior; no discount below the base
